summary: A 1977 proposed official standard for the format of ARPA Network messages. It was replaced by RFC 733.

plainLanguage.summary: This proposed one standard layout for network messages, like a form with fields for sender and subject. It was later replaced.

subtitle: Proposed official standard for the header format of ARPA Network messages (email).

tldr.problem: ARPANET message systems used informal or conflicting header formats, making it difficult for different systems to parse messages from each other.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 724 proposes an official standard for message headers with structured fields for addresses (using a special address syntax), metadata like date and subject, support for group mailing lists, and human-readable text that does not require parsing.
tldr.outcome: The standard attempted to unify ARPANET messaging, though it was later superseded by RFC 733. It introduced concepts like address groups and quoted-string syntax that became foundational to email standards.

facts.label: Required fields
facts.value: At least one message field (From, To, or Subject)

today: RFC 724 was a proposed standard. It was superseded by RFC 733.

sections.title: Background
sections.content: The ARPA Network used FTP commands (MAIL and MLFL) to send messages. RFC 561 (1971) had defined basic header fields like From, Date, and Subject, but as message systems grew more sophisticated, additional fields like To and Cc became standard without a formal specification. RFC 680 (1975) attempted to standardize these fields but received limited distribution. RFC 724 proposes a revised and officially-blessed standard that incorporates experience from both documents and addresses new requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Network mail started as a bolt-on feature for file transfer. As people used it more, they added fields like To and Cc without agreeing on the format, causing confusion.

sections.title: The Message Format
sections.content: A message consists of headers followed by a blank line and then the body text. Each header is a field name (like From:, To:, Subject:) followed by a field body. Address fields use a special syntax supporting individual mailboxes, groups (lists of people), and even non-network addresses like postal addresses. Headers can be folded across multiple lines by inserting whitespace on continuation lines. Field names are case-insensitive and may contain comments in parentheses.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a header section with fields for addresses, dates, and other metadata, written in a format that both people and programs can read.

sections.title: Address Syntax
sections.content: Addresses specify a mailbox (username plus host) or a group name that expands to multiple mailboxes. A mailbox is written as local-part@host and may be followed by a display name in parentheses or angle brackets. Groups allow nesting and include references to stored mailing lists. The syntax is designed to be readable by humans without special parsers, though formal syntax exists for programs that need to parse it strictly.
sections.plainLanguage: The address part says who the message is from or going to. It can be one person or many people in a group, and each address is written in a standard way.

references.text: Noel Chiappa, "Standardizing Network Mail Headers", RFC 561, September 1973.
Ken Pogran, David Crocker, John Vittal, Austin Henderson, "Message Transmission Protocol", RFC 680, 1975.
